Sadly, peak season for many fisheries directly overlaps with peak season for whales in those areas. 😩 Monterey Bay, CA is one of the places making good progress on this issue, and this year they got cleared to fish with pop-up gear. Here's a good write-up about it: usa.oceana.org/blog/a-win-w...

In our experience, many fishers are open to developing and using technology that will reduce entanglements (they don't want to lose their gear or harm whales either!), but it can be expensive, and in most places, such technology hasn't been legally approved for use yet. 🫤

@helloohart.bsky.social and @mushroomprince.bsky.social, wanted to clarify a couple of things. Entanglement is an issue with both commercial gear *and* recreational gear. This is not only a commercial fishing issue. Also, often the gear entangling whales was set properly and legally, not abandoned.

This ties in to why our endangered Southern Resident Killer Whales are struggling, too. They rely on fish and the fish populations are deeply affected by the changing oceans, human consumption, and environmental pressure on their natal streams.

It's all connected! 💕

Bigg's killer whales, on the other hand, eat marine mammals like seals, sea lions, and porpoises and there are an abundance of them in the territory that they roam, so they're able to deal with the changing ocean conditions more easily since they're nourished and they're bodies aren't as strained.

As warm waters affect the swaths of sea ice those crustacean populations aren't as reliable to find and the gray whales, who are already malnourished from the migration, have a hard time bulking up enough to sustain them longterm.

There are a lot of intersecting factors, but a lot of things that make the populations and their keys to survival very different

The key one here is food. Gray whales make a giant migration to the Arctic, relying on tiny crustaceans as their food source. Those crustaceans rely on sea ice to survive
